Welcome to the United Nations

The **2024 Revision of World Population Prospects** is the twenty-eighth edition of official United Nations population estimates and projections that have been prepared by the Population Division of the Department of Economic and Social Affairs of the United Nations Secretariat. It presents population estimates from 1950 to the present for 237 countries or areas, underpinned by analyses of historical demographic trends. This latest assessment considers the results of 1,910 national population censuses conducted between 1950 and 2023, as well as information from vital registration systems and from 3,189 nationally representative sample surveys. The 2024 revision also presents population projections to the year 2100 that reflect a range of plausible outcomes at the global, regional and national levels.

The main results are presented in a **series of Excel files** displaying key demographic indicators for each UN development group, World Bank income group, geographic region, Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) region, subregion and country or area for selected periods or dates within 1950-2100. An **online database (Data Portal)** provides access to a subset of key indicators and interactive data visualization, including an open API for programmatic access. For advanced users who need to use these data in a database form or statistical software, we recommend to use the **CSV format** for bulk download. **Special Aggregates** also provide additional groupings of countries (e.g., geographic, economic and trade, political, UN-related). Since the 2022 revision, the estimates and projections are presented in one-year intervals of age and time instead of the five-year intervals used previously. The various datasets disaggregated by age are available in two forms: by standard 5-year age groups and single ages.

Additional outputs, including results from the probabilistic projections, and more detailed metadata will be posted soon after the initial public release.

by H Ritchie · 2023 · Cited by 290 — Global population growth peaked in the 1960s at over 2% per year. Since then, rates have more than halved, falling to less than 1%.

When Nigeria became independent on October 1, 1960, the country that inherited sovereignty from Britain was very different from the Nigeria we know today.

There were no 36 states, no Abuja, no naira, no mobile phones and no internet. Oil had been discovered, but Nigeria was not yet an oil-dependent economy. Most Nigerians lived in rural communities, agriculture dominated the economy, and modern infrastructure was concentrated in a relatively small number of cities.

Yet this was not a country starting from nothing.

Nigeria had universities, newspapers, radio, television, banks, railways, ports, factories, hospitals, a growing professional class and a vibrant cultural scene.

So, what did the new nation actually look like?

Nigeria had a population of roughly 36 to 45 million people around independence, depending on the demographic estimate used. The uncertainty reflected the difficulties of conducting reliable population counts during the colonial period.

What is clearer is where most Nigerians lived.

The country was overwhelmingly rural. Historical United Nations-based estimates put the urban population at only about 15 per cent in 1960.

For most Nigerians, life revolved around farming, markets, villages, extended families, religious institutions and local communities. Cities were growing, but they were still small compared with the sprawling urban centres Nigerians know today.

The political map was also dramatically different.

At independence, Nigeria consisted principally of three large regions — Northern, Western and Eastern Nigeria — alongside the Federal Territory of Lagos.

The Northern Region was the largest geographically and had the largest population. The Western Region was centred largely around the Yoruba-speaking southwest, while the Eastern Region contained a large Igbo population alongside numerous other communities.

These regions were not politically or culturally identical, and regional competition was already a defining feature of Nigerian politics.

The Mid-Western Region did not exist yet; it was carved out of the Western Region in 1963.

There was also no Abuja. Lagos was the federal capital and the centre of national political and commercial life.

Lagos was already Nigeria’s principal political and commercial city, housing the Federal Government, Parliament, major businesses, the country’s leading port and much of its media activity.

But it was not the giant metropolis it is today.

Ibadan was a major political, commercial and educational centre in the West. Kano dominated commercial activity in the North and was closely linked to the region’s famous groundnut trade. Kaduna served as the administrative centre of Northern Nigeria, while Enugu was an important political and industrial city in the East.

Port Harcourt was emerging as a major commercial and port city, particularly as petroleum production began to develop.

Cities such as Benin, Onitsha, Aba, Jos, Zaria, Calabar, Abeokuta, Sokoto and Maiduguri were also important regional centres.

But beyond these urban hubs was a much larger rural Nigeria.

Nigeria at independence was fundamentally an agricultural economy.

Cocoa, groundnuts, palm oil, palm kernels, cotton, rubber, timber, hides and skins were among the country’s major commodities.

# Nigeria’s population soars, poverty soars

Columns 
December 15, 2020 12:24 am

Azuka Onwuka

By  Azuka Onwuka

Kindly share this story:

Last week, the National Population Commission announced that Nigeria’s population estimate had moved up to 206 million. The country’s population growth rate is put at about 2.6 per cent. In the last four years, Nigeria has experienced recession twice. Nigeria is still the country with the highest number of poor people, with 40 per cent of Nigerians living below the poverty line. Productivity has continued to dwindle. Insecurity has continued to rise.

 At independence in 1960, Nigeria had about 45 million people.  Twenty years later, its population was about 73 million. By 2000, the population had ballooned to about 122 million. And now at 2020, Nigeria has about 206 million people.

 Let us compare that to some other countries. Long before A.D. started 2,000 years ago, Greece was already established as a centre of intellectualism. Philosophers like Socrates, Plato and Aristotle had lived and died. Yet today, Greece as a country has a population of about 10 million.

Portugal was the first European country that interacted with the peoples of Nigeria. By the 15th century – long before the name “Nigeria” was coined by the British – the Portuguese had started doing business with the different indigenous peoples of what was to be later named Nigeria. Despite how long Portugal has reigned as a country, its population today is about 10 million.

Canada has been a developed and known country for centuries. It has the second largest land mass (second only to Russia). At 9,984,670 km2, Canada is almost 11 times the size of Nigeria. Canada has been welcoming thousands of immigrants every year. Yet, it has less than 40 million people.

The United Nations has projected that by 2050, Nigeria will be the third most populated country with a population of over 400 million. Yet, there is no similar growth projection about Nigeria’s food production, technological advancement, economic growth and the like. Nigerians are simply producing children thoughtlessly without any care about how this booming population will be fed and taken care of. More people but less productivity means hunger, anger, joblessness, crime and insecurity. Therefore, Nigeria is just running into extreme poverty and insecurity with her two eyes fully open.

Around 1986 when the erstwhile military dictator, Ibrahim Babangida, came up with the idea of each family having a maximum of four children as a means of checking population explosion, Nigerians reacted angrily. He clarified that it was merely an advisory and not a law. At that time, many people saw the idea of a family having only four children as outrageous. Having between six and nine children was in vogue.

Interestingly, in the Nigeria of today, especially in the South, that mindset has changed drastically. Anybody with six children today is viewed curiously as “a father of a nation!” Many families now have between two and three children. The idea is to give the children quality of life rather than having too many children that cannot be adequately catered for.
